title: Approved rubbers, colours and the racket rules
seo_title: ITTF racket rules: approved rubbers and colours
description: What makes a table tennis bat legal: ITTF-approved rubbers, the black and coloured sides, thickness limits, glue, racket testing and the rules in England.
summary: The blade can be almost any shape, but the rubbers on it are tightly controlled. Here is what makes a bat legal for league and tournament play, and how it is checked.
key_points: Any rubber used in competition must be on the ITTF's list of authorised racket coverings, with the ITTF logo visible near the handle.
One side must be black and the other a bright colour: red, or since October 2021 pink, violet, green or blue.
The blade can be any size, shape or weight, but must be flat, rigid and at least 85% natural wood.
Rubbers must be used as made: no boosters, no solvent glues, no treatment of any kind.
At major events rackets are tested before matches, and repeated failures can lead to a ban.
body: For league and tournament play, a bat (a racket, in the rules) is legal if each rubber is on the ITTF's list of authorised coverings and shows the ITTF logo near the handle, one side is black and the other a bright colour, the rubbers are within the thickness limits and have not been treated, and the blade is flat, rigid and mostly wood. A bat from a main brand with an "ITTF approved" label on the rubbers will meet these rules. For a game in the park, anything goes.

The ITTF, the world governing body, is relaxed about the blade. Law 2.4.1 says the racket "may be of any size, shape or weight but the blade shall be flat and rigid". At least 85% of its thickness must be natural wood. Layers of carbon or another fibre are allowed inside it, but each can be no thicker than 7.5% of the total or 0.35mm, whichever is less. Material may be added to shape the handle, and the part you grip may be left uncovered. Our guide to [blades explained](/guide/table-tennis-blades-explained.html) covers how they are built.

The rubbers are where the rules bite. Regulation 3.2.1.3 says every rubber must be "currently authorised by the ITTF" and attached so that "the ITTF logo, the ITTF number (when present), the supplier and brand names are clearly visible nearest the handle".

The authorised rubbers are set out in the ITTF's list of authorised racket coverings, known as the LARC, which since 2021 has been updated four times a year. Each rubber has its own ITTF number, printed next to the logo in a frame. If you are not sure about a rubber, look for the logo and number, and check the name against the current list. Rubbers that do not appear on it, including many cheap unbranded sheets, cannot be used in regulated competition.

Law 2.4.6 says the surface on one side must be black, and on the other "of a bright colour clearly distinguishable from black and from the colour of the ball". Both sides must be matt, not shiny. The rule lets your opponent see which rubber you are hitting with, which matters when the two sides play differently.

For decades the bright colour meant red. From 1 October 2021 the ITTF allowed pink, violet, green and blue as well. One side must still be black, so a pink and green bat is not allowed. A side left without rubber must still be matt and the right colour, but you cannot hit the ball with it: Law 2.10.1.8 gives the point to your opponent if you strike the ball with a side that does not meet the covering rules.

Each side you hit with must be covered either with ordinary pimpled rubber, a single sheet with the pimples outwards and no sponge, or with sandwich rubber, a sheet of pimpled rubber on one layer of sponge. Under the 2026 Laws, ordinary pimpled rubber must be less than 2.05mm thick including the glue, and sandwich rubber less than 4.05mm, with the pimpled top sheet no more than 2mm. The rubber must be of even thickness and must reach "up to but not beyond the limits of the blade". Our guides to [rubbers](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) and [sponge thickness](/guide/rubber-sponge-thickness-hardness.html) explain what the different types do.

Law 2.4.7 says the covering "shall be used without any physical, chemical or other treatment". The Regulations spell it out: a rubber must be used exactly as the ITTF authorised it, without changing its "playing properties, friction, outlook, colour, structure, surface", and "no additives shall be used". That rules out boosters and oils, and the speed glues that players once brushed on before matches, which were banned in 2008. The ITTF said in 2019 that "chemicals must stay in the hands of the professional manufacturing companies".

Glue is the player's responsibility. Regulation 3.2.4.1 says rubbers must be attached with adhesives that "do not contain harmful volatile solvents". The water-based glues sold by the main makers are made for this; our guide to [building a custom bat](/guide/custom-vs-ready-made-bats.html) shows how to use them.
## Checks before and during a match

Before a match, and whenever you change bats during one, you must show your racket to your opponent and the umpire and let them examine it. You cannot swap bats during a match unless yours is accidentally damaged so badly that it cannot be used; if you change it for any other reason, the umpire stops play and calls the referee. Between games you leave your bat on the table unless the umpire says otherwise.

At World Championships, the Olympics and Paralympics and some other ITTF events, a racket control centre tests bats before matches for flatness, rubber thickness, even layers and harmful or volatile substances. A bat that fails cannot be used, though a second one may be tested in its place. Players who fail four times in four years are suspended for 12 months. You can also ask for your bat to be tested voluntarily, with no penalty.

Table Tennis England uses the ITTF Laws, and its byelaws make the same rules on authorised rubbers and changing rackets mandatory in regulated competitions: tournaments and leagues it or its affiliated organisations authorise. Internal club competitions are not regulated competitions, so your club may be more relaxed on club nights, but a local league match is likely to be regulated. If you are about to join one, our guide to [finding a club and a league](/guide/find-a-table-tennis-club-england.html) is the next step.
